title: ペストは今も消えていない — アフリカとアメリカで毎年報告
title_zh: 鼠疫一直没消失，非洲和美国几乎每年都有病例
lead: 14世紀のヨーロッパで何千万人もの命を奪ったペスト。でも、この病気は今も世界に残っています。アフリカやアメリカでは、今でも毎年患者が出ているそうです。
lead_zh: 14世纪在欧洲夺走数千万人性命的鼠疫，其实至今仍存在于世界上。据说非洲和美国现在每年都还有病例出现。

preview_zh: 很多人可能以为鼠疫是过去的事。但据世界卫生组织（WHO）说，从1990年代到现在，人类病例报告最多的地方是非洲。尤其是刚果和马达加斯加好像特别多。在美国，平均每年也有大约7个病例，大多在美国西部的农村地区。
paragraphs: ペストは、昔の話だと思っている人が多いかもしれません。しかし、世界保健機関（WHO）によると、1990年代から今まで、人間の患者が一番多く報告されているのはアフリカです。特にコンゴとマダガスカルで多いそうです。アメリカでも、毎年平均7人ぐらいの患者が出ています。ほとんどが西部の田舎の地域です。
ペストを起こすのは、エルシニア・ペスティスという細菌です。この細菌は、プレーリードッグやネズミなどのげっ歯類の間で広がります。そして、感染した動物から飛び移ったノミが人をかむと、人も病気になります。
ペストにはいくつかの種類があります。一番多いのは腺ペストで、リンパ節がひどくはれて、痛くなります。ほかにも、肺がおかされる肺ペストと、血液がおかされる敗血症ペストがあります。早く治療しないと、どちらも命に関わることがあります。
人から人へうつることもあります。肺ペストの人がせきをすると、そのしぶきで近くの人にうつる可能性があります。でも、イギリスの大学のサイモン・クラークさんは「人と動物の距離が近いから、細菌を完全になくすのは難しい」と話します。
昔と違って、今は抗生物質で治せます。大切なのは、早く医者に行くことです。ワクチンもありますが、WHOは研究施設や病院で働く人など、感染の危険が高い人だけにすすめています。
最近、シベリアの研究所で働く人が亡くなり、ロシアで心配の声が上がりました。ただ、ロシアの当局は「ペストの証拠はなかった」と説明しています。
paragraphs_zh: 很多人可能以为鼠疫是过去的事。但据世界卫生组织（WHO）说，从1990年代到现在，人类病例报告最多的地方是非洲。尤其是刚果和马达加斯加好像特别多。在美国，平均每年也有大约7个病例，大多在美国西部的农村地区。
引起鼠疫的是一种叫鼠疫耶尔森菌的细菌。这种细菌在土拨鼠、老鼠等啮齿类动物之间传播。然后，从感染的动物身上跳过来的跳蚤咬了人，人也会得病。
鼠疫有好几种类型。最常见的是腺鼠疫，会让淋巴结严重肿痛。此外还有肺部受影响的肺鼠疫，以及血液受影响的败血型鼠疫。如果不早点治疗，这两种都可能危及生命。
鼠疫也可能人传人。肺鼠疫患者咳嗽时，飞沫可能会传染给附近的人。不过，英国大学的西蒙·克拉克先生说：“因为人和动物离得近，所以很难把这种细菌彻底消灭。”
和过去不同，现在可以用抗生素治好。关键是尽早去看医生。虽然有疫苗，但WHO只建议在研究所、医院工作等感染风险高的人接种。
最近，西伯利亚一家研究所的工作人员去世，在俄罗斯引发了担忧。不过，俄罗斯当局解释说：“没有发现鼠疫的证据。”

title_original: The plague never went away. Cases are reported in parts of Africa and the US nearly every year
summary_original: The plague, the rare bacterial infection infamously known for killing tens of millions in 14th-century Europe, never went away. It is now easily treated with antibiotics.

The plague, the rare bacterial infection infamously known for killing tens of millions in 14th-century Europe, never went away. It is now easily treated with antibiotics.
Since the 1990s, most human cases have been reported in Africa, especially Congo and Madagascar, according to the
World Health Organization
.
There are an average of about seven human cases per year in the U.S.,
according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
, mostly in rural areas of the American West.
A worker at a plague research institute in Siberia recently died of pneumonia.
The case has raised alarm
in Russia after unconfirmed media reports suggested she might have died of pneumonic plague. Russian authorities say testing showed no evidence of plague, but the research institute has been quarantined.
"People think the plague is gone, it was something that occurred 500 years ago. It's not. It's here amongst us," said Simon Clarke of the University of Reading in the U.K. "Unless you get rid of those wild animals, which of course is not possible, then you're not going to get rid of the bacteria."
Surprised to hear the plague is still around? Here's what to know.
Plague can attack lymph nodes, lungs and blood
People in Siberia have been dying of plague for at least 5,500 years. The earliest evidence of a form of the disease was
found in teeth from ancient hunter-gatherers
north of the region's Lake Baikal.
Pneumonic plague and the more well-known bubonic plague—also called the Black Death—are caused by the same bacteria, called Yersinia pestis.
The bacteria spread naturally among rodents like prairie dogs and rats. Fleas that jump from infected animals and bite people can spread the disease.
The bubonic plague is the most common form of the infection. It causes painfully swollen lymph nodes that are most commonly found in the groin, armpit and neck, called buboes. Other symptoms include sudden high fever and chills, headaches, and pain in the abdomen, legs and arms, according to the Cleveland Clinic.
There are two other forms of the plague: pneumonic plague, which can be caused by inhaling the bacteria, infects the lungs, while septicemic plague is an infection in the bloodstream. Both are fatal if not treated early, according to the World Health Organization.
Bubonic plague will often develop into the other two forms of plague if untreated.
Plague can spread through fleas or bodily fluids
Other than bites from infected fleas, people can also get plague by touching infected bodily fluids, so health experts recommend taking extra care when handling dead or sick animals.
The plague can also spread through the respiratory droplets of someone who has pneumonic plague.
"If you cough, you can spread it to another person, but that doesn't travel very far," said Dr. Glenn Wortmann, MedStar Washington Hospital Center. "So you really need to be in face-to-face contact with that person to get pneumonic plague."
That's why "the chance of this spreading widely in Russia and then extending here to the U.S. will not happen," he said.
Antibiotics can treat plague
The plague was never eradicated, but we've gotten better at preventing its spread and treating it in humans.
When treated early with antibiotics, the plague can be cured. The key is to get to a doctor fast—otherwise the plague can be deadly.
There is a vaccine, but the WHO only recommends it for people who are at high risk of infection, like laboratory and healthcare workers. There isn't strong evidence that vaccines can work against the pneumonic form.
There's no plague vaccine available in the U.S.
